newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's verbal support for yen pushes down dollar.
newsitem.headline: Japan's verbal support for yen pushes down dollar.

text.p: Japan kept up its steady stream of comments in support of the yen on Friday, helping to push the dollar below 123 yen for the first time in more than a month.

The greenback, undermined by signs that its two-year rally may be ending, was hovering just below 123 yen in late afternoon trade in Tokyo after earlier falling as low as 122.56 yen. It traded at around 123.75 in late New York on Thursday.

The U.S. currency weakened in early trade, undermined by speculation over the possibility of higher Japanese interest rates and by a comment by Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka expressing hope that a currency agreement by the Group of Seven (G7) nations in late April would be "further digested" by the markets.

The dollar had already suffered a body blow on Thursday when Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara, known as "Mr Yen" for the influence he exerts in the currency markets, said it could drop to 103 yen.

Financial leaders from the G7 -- Japan, the United States, Germany, Britain, France, Italy and Canada -- said in Washington last month that they would monitor exchange rates and cooperate as appropriate. They said currency values should reflect fundamentals and excess volatility was undesirable.

U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, speaking in New York after Mitsuzuka's remark, briefly pushed up the dollar with comments traders took to imply that further rises in U.S. interest rates were possible.

But the dollar eased again after Mitsuzuka told a parliamentary panel Japan would intervene to stabilise currencies if market moves were excessive and that to be effective, intervention should be done jointly with other nations.
Sakakibara later reiterated Japan's determination to do battle against "excessive" currency swings.

The market is sensitive to official comments and the possibility of central bank intervention because factors such as Japan's growing current account surplus and capital flows suggest a weaker dollar anyway. In fact, some analysts said Japan's verbal intervention might succeed sufficiently to make actual dollar-selling by central banks unnecessary.
A weak yen helps keep Japan's economic recovery on track by boosting exports, but rising exports and a growing current account surplus could fan trade friction with Washington.
This, in turn, could spark a yen surge that could seriously undermine Japanese corporate competitiveness.

"I think what (the Japanese) are doing is showing they are making every effort possible to avoid growth through exports and so diffuse political pressure when the trade surplus starts to expand," said Kenneth Landon, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "Generally, when the U.S. really starts beating up (on Japan), we really see the yen take off."

Speculation that the Bank of Japan might at long last tighten its hyper-easy credit stance because of greater confidence in the economic recovery also undermined the dollar and sparked a sharp drop in Japanese government bond prices.

Japan's Economic Planning Agency said in its monthly economic report that the economy was recovering gradually and a sales tax rise from three percent to five percent from April 1 was not hurting much.
Some economists said they did not expect a quick credit tightening, given uncertainty about domestic growth and worries about the bad-loan burden at some Japanese banks.
The Bank of Japan slashed its official discount rate, at which it lends to commercial banks, to a record-low 0.5 percent in September 1995 to help keep the economy from slumping.
